Building the quadruped

I’m developing a twelve-joint quadruped with teammates, from the printed mechanisms to the software that controls each leg.

Assembly and testing have exposed problems that were easy to miss in CAD. My work includes revising the body, leg structures, and actuator interfaces, developing analytical leg models, and moving from Python prototypes to C++ control.

How the CAD evolved

  1. Early team design

    Build the layout around modular joints

    The early team CAD established how the actuators, legs, and body would fit together.

  2. Assembly review

    Make the geometry practical to assemble

    The project review identified difficult countersunk-bolt access, bulky hip structures, tight fits, and missing provisions for batteries, electronics, and wiring. Those problems guided the next revisions.

  3. August–September 2026 captures

    Open the frame and revisit the joint structure

    In later revisions, I worked on an open frame and revised joint structures, considering material removal, bearing seats, wiring access, and serviceability.

These images document the team’s CAD revisions, dated by capture. The printed component appears in the hardware section below.

Printing and checking the frame

I compare the CAD with what can be printed and assembled, then examine how the part behaves under load. Fit, fastener access, print direction, and local stiffness each need attention.

Working through the leg geometry

I started with geometric forward and inverse kinematics, then worked through the Jacobian using component derivatives and homogeneous transforms. My handwritten revisions show the calculations and corrections along the way.

Testing one leg at a time

I worked through joint-direction signs, encoder references, gear ratios, and CAN communication during staged leg tests. Teammates helped with assembly and subsystems such as IMU communication. Clear interfaces helped us trace whether a problem came from the mechanism, coordinate conventions, or communication.

Results and current work

PROJECT STATUS

Hardware built; reliable walking is still in development.

The project has produced coordinated leg trajectories and limited locomotion. I’m still working toward reliable forward walking and terrain traversal. The robot uses off-the-shelf motor drivers; our first custom controller PCB did not operate successfully.
